blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Egocentric video supports diverse applications, including robot learning, augmented reality, and human activity understanding. Recovering metric 3D hand trajectories from such video requires estimating both hand motion and camera egomotion to express the hands in a consistent reference frame. Many existing pipelines recover hand and camera motion in separate stages, combining hand detection, hand reconstruction, camera tracking, and trajectory refinement. We present V-JEPA Hand, a simple feed-forward video model that jointly reconstructs bilateral hand motion and camera motion from egocentric clips. It uses a self-supervised V-JEPA 2.1 encoder to extract spatio-temporal features from full-frame video and a query-based predictor to decode these features into per-frame hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion. We use the predicted camera motion to express the hand trajectories in a common world frame. The model accepts known focal lengths or predicts them when unavailable. It reconstructs each clip in a single forward pass. We train both components end to end in a single stage on a mixture of diverse pseudo-labelled videos and high-precision 3D annotations. A single model achieves the lowest coverage-aware mean per-joint position error (MPJPE) among comparable baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D, and EgoStandard. It also yields lower world-frame trajectory errors than the compared SLAM-based pipelines. Ablations support the benefits of video pretraining, temporal context, and mixed supervision. V-JEPA Hand achieves a forward-pass throughput of 93.4 FPS on a single RTX A6000. Project page: https://qft-333.github.io/V-JEPA-Hand-Page/.

consistent reference frame therefore requires estimating both hands’
positions, orientations, finger articulation, and presence, together with

Single-image models such as HaMeR and
WiLoR ( Pavlakos et al., 2024 ; Potamias et al., 2025 ) reconstruct hands from
detected crops. Applied frame by frame, they cannot use neighboring frames
to improve reconstruction under occlusion, motion blur, or intermittent
visibility. Temporal methods add
cross-frame modeling ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , while world-frame approaches
combine hand reconstruction with camera tracking, motion infilling, or
optimization ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Chen and others, 2025 ) . More recently, ViDiHand ( Wang et al., 2026 ) uses pretrained video diffusion features for
detector-free, full-frame hand reconstruction. Video provides temporal cues for hand reconstruction and scene context for
camera motion.
We further investigate how effectively a self-supervised video encoder can
support joint hand–camera recovery through end-to-end, single-stage
adaptation .

blocks.en:
Our central finding is that a simple video encoder–predictor
architecture can achieve accurate and fast joint hand–camera reconstruction .
We instantiate this design as V-JEPA Hand, pairing the self-supervised
V-JEPA 2.1 encoder ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) with a query-based predictor
and fine-tuning both end to end. Cross-frame information is incorporated
within the visual encoder, and hand and camera states are decoded from the
same spatio-temporal features. The predictor jointly estimates
per-frame bilateral hand poses, hand presence, and camera motion; it also
accepts known clip-level focal lengths or predicts them when unavailable.
The entire clip is reconstructed in one forward pass without a separate
hand detector, hand crops, SLAM, or test time optimization. The model thus
retains a simple feedforward structure rather than assembling estimates from
independent hand and camera systems.

blocks.en:
Training such a model requires accurate 3D annotations across diverse
capture conditions. ARCTIC ( Fan et al., 2023 ) and
HOT3D ( Banerjee et al., 2024 ) provide high-quality hand-motion annotations
using dedicated motion-capture systems, while H2O ( Kwon et al., 2021 ) uses
calibrated multi-view RGB-D recordings to annotate bimanual interactions.
These resources provide valuable geometric supervision, but their hardware
and calibration requirements make collection costly to extend across
everyday environments. In contrast, Ego4D ( Grauman et al., 2022 ) and
EPIC-KITCHENS ( Damen et al., 2018 ) capture diverse, unscripted
activities without dense metric hand-motion labels. Reconstruction offers a
complementary source of supervision: HaWoR ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) recovers
world-space hand trajectories, while the VITRA annotation
pipeline ( Li et al., 2025 ) combines hand reconstruction with metric camera
tracking to generate frame-aligned hand-action labels at scale. Such
automatically recovered trajectories are useful but imperfect pseudo-labels.
We therefore train in a single stage on pseudo-labelled Ego4D and our
in-house recordings, mixed with a comparatively small pool of precisely
annotated videos from ARCTIC and HOT3D. The pseudo-labelled videos broaden
scene and action coverage, while the high-quality annotations provide
reliable geometric supervision for transfer beyond the capture environments.

We evaluate the same trained model on ARCTIC ( Fan et al., 2023 ) ,

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Estimating 3D hand pose and shape from monocular images has advanced rapidly
with parametric models such as MANO ( Romero et al., 2017 ) .
Most existing methods detect then regress, cropping
each hand with a 2D detector before predicting mesh or kinematic
parameters ( Pavlakos et al., 2024 ; Potamias et al., 2025 ; Dong et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2022 ; Moon, 2023 ; Park et al., 2022 ) .
In egocentric videos, however, this pipeline struggles with frequent occlusions,
motion blur, and boundary truncations, while discarding global context and
inter-hand spatial relations.
To bypass cropping, detector-free alternatives directly regress hand poses from
full frames ( Prakash et al., 2024 ) or leverage video diffusion
features ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , though diffusion models incur substantial
computational overhead.
In contrast, V-JEPA Hand recovers both hands and their presence probabilities in a
single forward pass via a lightweight query-based decoder, avoiding separate
detectors, crops, or iterative diffusion.

blocks.en:
Applying single-frame estimators independently across video frames yields
temporally jittery trajectories. While temporal networks and transformers help
smooth camera-relative predictions ( Yang et al., 2020 ; Zhang et al., 2024 ) ,
they do not resolve camera egomotion.
To express manipulation in a consistent world frame, current methods decouple
hand estimation from camera tracking by combining per-frame regressors,
external visual SLAM such as DROID-SLAM ( Teed and Deng, 2021 ) , and motion
infilling or test-time trajectory
optimization ( Zhang et al., 2025 ; Chen and others, 2025 ; Fan et al., 2024 ) , mirroring
pipelines in world-grounded body capture ( Ye et al., 2023 ; Shin et al., 2024 ) .
However, SLAM frequently drifts under aggressive head motion, and multi-stage
optimization introduces latency and cascading errors.
Instead, V-JEPA Hand unifies camera-space bilateral hand motion, hand presence,
camera egomotion, and camera intrinsics into a single feedforward prediction,
avoiding external SLAM or test-time optimization while achieving superior
world-frame accuracy.

blocks.en:
Self-supervised video pretraining provides powerful motion and scene priors.
While masked autoencoders such as MAE ( He et al., 2022 ) ,
VideoMAE ( Tong et al., 2022 ) , and VideoMAE V2 ( Wang et al., 2023 ) reconstruct masked pixels, pixel-level objectives often overemphasize
high-frequency texture details over geometric and physical dynamics.
The Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA)
family ( Assran et al., 2023 ; Bardes et al., 2024 ; Assran et al., 2025 ; Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) addresses this by predicting representations in latent space; notably,
V-JEPA 2.1 ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) learns rich spatio-temporal features
and dense motion priors.
Although generative video foundation models ( Blattmann et al., 2023 ) also
encode temporal priors ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , their generative nature requires heavy
computation.
In comparison, V-JEPA 2.1 offers a discriminative representation that supports
high-throughput ( 91.3 91.3 FPS) inference and outperforms VideoMAE,
DINOv3 ( Siméoni et al., 2025 ) , and Perception Encoder ( Bolya et al., 2025 ) on
both camera- and world-frame metrics.

blocks.en: 3 Method
blocks.zh: 3 方法

blocks.en:
As illustrated in Figure 2 , V-JEPA Hand reads a raw video clip and
emits, in a single forward pass, the complete bilateral hand trajectory of that
clip together with the camera motion and focal lengths.
The model has two components: a self-supervised video encoder that turns the
clip into a spatio-temporal token grid (Section 3.2 ), and a
query-based trajectory predictor that decodes one output token per frame into
the per-frame state defined below. Section 3.3 describes
our single-stage training with multi-source supervision, combining large-scale
pseudo-labelled video with high-quality data under a shared
training objective.

blocks.en: 3.3 Training
blocks.zh: 3.3 培训

blocks.en:
We train V-JEPA Hand end to end in a single stage using four datasets:
Ego4D ( Grauman et al., 2022 ) , our in-house egocentric recordings,
ARCTIC ( Fan et al., 2023 ) , and HOT3D ( Banerjee et al., 2024 ) .
We process Ego4D and our in-house recordings with the VITRA annotation
pipeline ( Li et al., 2025 ) to obtain a large-scale pool of pseudo-labelled
video spanning diverse scenes, activities, and camera wearers.
We mix this noisy pseudo-labelled data with high-quality data from the
training splits of ARCTIC and HOT3D.
Throughout training, each clip is sampled from the pseudo-labelled pool,
ARCTIC, or HOT3D with probabilities 0.35 0.35 , 0.45 0.45 , and 0.20 0.20 , respectively.

We evaluate on three egocentric hand benchmarks: ARCTIC tests reconstruction under severe
occlusion during two-hand object manipulation, while HOT3D tests robustness to motion blur
from rapid head and hand movements. We additionally evaluate on EgoStandard , a commercially annotated egocentric dataset spanning
diverse scenes. Its 3D motion annotations are produced by a pipeline that
combines hardware-assisted capture with multi-stage optimization. We exclude
EgoStandard entirely from training and use it to assess generalization to
unseen egocentric data.
The EgoStandard evaluation covers approximately 60 60 minutes of video.
For HOT3D, we follow the HaWoR validation split, covering approximately 49 49 minutes of video.

with all world methods rescored on their common true-positive support.

Adding the pseudo-labelled Ego4D and in-house data helps the model place

The benefit is not simply that the model detects more hands—detection

Instead, the broader training data improves the geometry of the reconstruction

less accurate. The two terms therefore serve different purposes: one
discourages temporal jumps, while the other keeps the reconstruction
consistent with the image.

Table 6 changes one choice at a time: starting the encoder
from random weights, freezing its pretrained weights, or replacing the video
input with a single frame. The remaining training setup is shared.
Training from scratch gives much less accurate poses and world trajectories
on both benchmarks. Even a frozen pretrained encoder performs substantially
better, and fine-tuning it improves the results further. Thus, pretraining
provides useful features for hand reconstruction, while task-specific training
helps the model make better use of them.
Single-frame predictions remain reasonably accurate in each image, but
are much less smooth over time. Seeing neighboring frames therefore helps
not only with pose accuracy, but also with keeping successive predictions
consistent.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
We presented V-JEPA Hand, a simple model that jointly reconstructs bilateral
hand motion, camera motion and intrinsics from egocentric video in one forward
pass, without hand detection, SLAM or test-time optimization. Built on
V-JEPA 2.1 and trained in a single stage on mixed pseudo-labelled and
high-quality data, it achieves the lowest coverage-aware MPJPE among reproduced
baselines on ARCTIC, HOT3D and the unseen EgoStandard benchmark, and lower
world-frame MPJPE than SLAM-based pipelines. Ablations show that mixing in
pseudo-labelled video improves generalization, and validate video pretraining,
temporal context and encoder choice. Running at over 90 90 frames per second,
V-JEPA Hand enables large-scale bilateral hand-motion annotation of egocentric
video to support robot imitation learning in embodied AI.

Figure 5 visualizes encoder features after
end-to-end training for hand and camera trajectory recovery.
V-JEPA 2.1 learns dense representations that capture fine-grained spatial
structure as well as global visual information ( Mur-Labadia et al., 2026 ) .
Our visualizations suggest that meaningful spatial and semantic structure
remains present after task-specific training: regions corresponding to
hands and forearms form coherent feature patterns, while manipulated
objects and surrounding surfaces often exhibit distinct patterns.
These observations are consistent with retaining semantically structured
features while adapting the encoder to geometric prediction.

For the hand tracks selected above, Table 2 reports joint
position errors (W-MPJPE and WA-MPJPE) and relative wrist trajectory error
(RTE), evaluated over the full clip.
Before measuring errors, we align the predicted hand trajectory to the
ground truth using one rotation and translation for the whole track.
This rigid alignment does not change scale or adjust frames independently.
The metrics differ in how this alignment is estimated and which errors
are measured: • W-MPJPE: align at the start. We fit the rotation and translation using the 21 21 predicted and
ground-truth hand joints in the first evaluated frame, then apply that
same transformation to every evaluated frame.

evaluated frames, including the first frame, in millimetres.
This measures how well the reconstruction follows the ground truth
after the initial alignment. • WA-MPJPE: align the whole track. We instead fit a single rotation and translation using the corresponding
joints from all evaluated frames together.

its first evaluated frame. • RTE: normalize wrist error by motion magnitude. Using the whole-track alignment from WA-MPJPE, we compute the mean
Euclidean distance between predicted and ground-truth wrist positions.

wrist moves from its position in the first evaluated frame, and multiply
by 100 100 to obtain a percentage. The denominator is a displacement
from the starting position, not the total distance travelled.

RTE to avoid dividing by a near-zero motion magnitude; they remain
included in W-MPJPE and WA-MPJPE.

models’ common true-positive hand-frames and the full-track metrics

blocks.en: G.3 Encoder configurations
blocks.zh: G.3 编码器配置

blocks.en:
We use the same ViT-L backbone scale and self-attention predictor design,
and match the number of temporal token groups across encoders.
V-JEPA 2.1 and VideoMAE use 16 16 input frames with two-frame tubelets,
whereas DINOv3 and PE-Spatial use 8 8 independently encoded frames,
yielding eight temporal groups in both cases. This keeps the number of
temporal groups passed to the predictor consistent, although the spatial
grids and input durations differ. Output query counts
match the input frame counts. The configured training image size is 384 384 for V-JEPA 2.1 and 224 224 for the alternatives; PE-Spatial’s positional grid
is interpolated from its pretrained 448 448 -pixel configuration.
For DINOv3 and PE-Spatial, frames
are processed as a batch of images, prefix tokens are removed, and patch
tokens are concatenated in temporal order for the predictor. Temporal
attention is therefore learned in the predictor rather than applied within
the image backbone.
